requirements.requirement: node1 and node2 share a single virtual IP (10.100.40.200) on the private network, only one answering at a time
requirements.summary: keepalived VRRP configured identically on both OpenWrt nodes (same virtual_router_id 51, VIP 10.100.40.200/24 on br-lan), with node1 priority 150 (MASTER) and node2 priority 100 (BACKUP). After starting keepalived, node1 held the VIP (cmd-c217e053bda44f9e) while node2 did not (cmd-80bd66ca628f4063), confirming exclusive single ownership.

requirements.requirement: When one node stops serving the VIP, the other takes it over automatically
requirements.summary: After stopping keepalived on node1 (cmd-2e3e0f0549a849ab), node2 acquired the VIP within the observation window without manual intervention (cmd-223671c51ea44780), demonstrating automatic VRRP failover.

requirements.requirement: node3 keeps reaching the shared VIP across one such failover transition
requirements.summary: A healthy baseline was directly observed (node3 pinged the VIP with 0% loss while node1 was MASTER, cmd-0252e152b9394ff6). A continuous 0.3s-interval ping from node3 was started (cmd-90bb7b34a639480b) and running when node1's keepalived was stopped; log analysis (cmd-092b4e574047488f, cmd-7dcb8c73a1fc4e96) shows only 2 packets (seq 15-16, matching an approx 1.4s RTT spike to 537ms/237ms) lost during the transition, with sequence numbers continuing unbroken and no gaps, then resuming to node2 as the new VIP holder. This is a direct, bounded, before/during/after observation of the required transition.

requirements.requirement: Redundancy pair returns to a healthy state after the disruption (not explicitly required by the instruction, but reasonable follow-through)
requirements.summary: keepalived was restarted on node1 and it preempted the VIP back due to higher priority (cmd-d01612961a674171); node2 released it and returned to BACKUP without the VIP (cmd-8b844a1deb1142b0), confirming the pair returned to its designed roles.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task instruction — a single shared VIP on the node1/node2 pair, automatic failover, and node3's continued reachability across a real, bounded transition — are directly and coherently evidenced. The failover window was captured with a continuous ping log showing only ~2 lost packets during the actual handover, which is strong direct proof rather than inferred configuration. Failback was also demonstrated, restoring the pair to its designed MASTER/BACKUP state. The mandatory provider-wide node-restart protocol was executed on all three nodes with pre/post boot-id capture and recovered state; node2 and node3 boot-identity changes are independently corroborated by the fixed after-executor snapshot, but the after-executor snapshot's boot-identity probe for node1 failed (return_code 255, empty output) even though other node1 checks in the same snapshot succeeded moments later, so node1's post-reboot boot-id could not be independently cross-checked (only the executor's own capture, cmd-e8bb5326439a4d84, evidences it). This does not contradict the executor's claim, and restart/persistence was not itself part of the public task contract, so it does not reduce the outcome scores, but it is noted as a limitation lowering confidence slightly. No unnecessary or unexplained mutations were found; the one failed troubleshooting command left no residue and was promptly corrected.
limitations: The fixed after-executor snapshot's boot-identity probe for node1 returned an empty result with return_code 255, so the required independent cross-check of node1's final post-reboot boot identity could not be completed from the fixed lifecycle data alone — only the executor's own captured boot_id (575791ba...) is available for that specific claim.

The before_prepare and after_prepare snapshots are identical (prepare stage was disabled), so no prepare-vs-executor delta analysis was possible beyond the raw before/after-executor diff already reviewed.

operational_hygiene.summary: State-changing executor commands were tightly scoped to the task: package installs (apk add keepalived on node1/node2), UCI config commits, keepalived start/stop for the failover demonstration (bounded and fully restored by cmd-d01612961a674171/cmd-8b844a1deb1142b0), and the three sequential reboots required by the provider-wide restart protocol. One troubleshooting attempt (cmd-aac0d5003cdd4066, a 'nohup sh -c sleep 1; reboot' background job) failed harmlessly because nohup is not present in the OpenWrt busybox environment ('/bin/sh: nohup: not found' in /tmp/reboot.log, confirmed by cmd-bb08287e34444e2b) — it produced no actual reboot or other state mutation, and the executor corrected course with a working 'sh -c' variant (cmd-cd9bc4a856c84eb3). No abandoned files, conflicting services, unsafe exposure, or broken package state were introduced; the after-executor snapshot only shows expected keepalived-related additions (config files, lock/pid files, uci-defaults entries) on node1/node2 with no unexplained residue. The listening-sockets diff on node1 is fully explained by the DNS service binding to the new VIP interface, not by unrelated exposure.
